extracted.intended_audience: editors, authors, copyeditors, proofreaders, and typesetters
extracted.subtask_description: A manual of editorial style focused on punctuation (commas, apostrophes, dashes, parentheses, brackets, ellipses, hyphens), rules for word divisions (hyphenation at line breaks), language-specific division rules, and footnote/index formatting for scholarly publishing and typesetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma usage in dates, signatures, and openings (161)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the comma between month and year in certain journals; omit the comma in signatures and at the beginning of articles after an author's name followed by address, title, or position in a separate line, or after an address followed by a date line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Journal and Botanical Gazette do not use a comma between month and year; omit comma after author's name when followed by address or title on a separate line (see related rule 65).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma placement with quotation marks and parentheses (162)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is always placed inside quotation marks; if a parenthesis follows, the comma follows the quotation but comes after the closing parenthesis when context requires it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place commas inside quotation marks even when a parenthesis follows; treat punctuation relative to closing quotation and parentheses according to context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophes in contractions (163)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an apostrophe to mark omitted letters in contractions and omitted figures in numbers; in contractions of verb + negative, do not use a space between components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: it's, ne'er, 'twas, "takin' me 'at"; the class of '96; don't, haven't. (See also rule 123.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of the possessive case (164)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the possessive of common and proper nouns by adding an apostrophe, or apostrophe + s as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man's word; horses' tails; Scott's Ivanhoe; Jones's farms; Themistocles' era; for appearance' sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural of numerals and rare/artificial coinages (165)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the plural of numerals and of rare or artificially coined nouns with an apostrophe + s; for monosyllabic proper names ending in a sibilant, add an apostrophe alone; other proper names add s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in the 1900's; in two's and three's; the three R's; the Y.M.C.A.'s; "these I-just-do-as-I-please's"; "all the Tommy Atkins' of England" (but: the Rosses and the Macdougals); the Pericles' and Socrates' of literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dashes to indicate sudden breaks or emphatic pauses (166)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an em dash to denote a sudden break, stop, or transition in a sentence, an abrupt change in construction, a long pause, or an epigrammatic turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Do we — can we — send out educated boys and girls..."; "To be or not to be — that is the question". Quoted examples illustrate dramatic or emphatic separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dashes for parenthetical clauses independent in logic and structure (167)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dashes (rarely parentheses) to set off parenthetical clauses that are both logically and structurally independent interpolations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "This may be said to be — but, never mind, we will pass over that"; "There came a time — let us say, for convenience... — when this attention..." (See rule 150 for parenthetical guidance.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash to introduce emphasis or repetition (168)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a clause that repeats a word or phrase from the main clause for emphasis or explanation by a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "the sources for history — the history of events and ideas"; "a new and difficult problem — new and difficult, that is, in the sense that..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dash when "namely" is implied (169)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer a dash before a parenthetical or complementary clause when a 'namely' is implied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "These discoveries — gunpowder, printing-press, compass, and telescope —"; "another division of our field — the interpretation of New Testament books."

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash before a final summarizing clause (170)
rubrics_metrics.description: In sentences broken into clauses, precede the final summarizing clause with a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: list of prophets ending with a summarizing clause preceded by an em dash to introduce the summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash after separate-line headings or single words followed by paragraphs (171)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a word or phrase is set on a separate line and the following paragraphs are implied by it, follow that line with a dash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example structure: "I recommend — "i. That we kill him. 2. That we flay him."

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash with side-heads and run-in headings (172)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a dash in connection with side-heads, whether run-in or paragraphed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "The language of the New Testament. — The lexicons of Grimm-Thayer..."; use dashes similarly in notes and side-head contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: En dash vs em dash for ranges and connections (173)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a dash (en or em as appropriate) to connect words or numbers (replacing the word 'to'); use en dash for month ranges and hyphen/en dash conventions for page ranges, and do not replace 'to' when the construction includes 'from'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: May–July, 1906 (en dash); May 1, 1905 — November 1, 1906 (em dash); pp. 3–7 (en dash); Luke 3:6 — 5:2 (em dash). But: 'From May 1 to July 1, 1906.' On consecutive numbers omit hundreds in the second number (1880-95), except some journals repeat hundreds (Astrophysical Journal and Botanical Gazette).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dash preceding references after full direct quotations in notes (174)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a dash precede the reference (author/title) following a direct quotation of at least one complete sentence in footnotes or when cited independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show a dash linking a quotation and its citation: '... such an instance of civic heroism.' — Thirty Years, I, 379.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on dash use with other punctuation (175)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not ordinarily use a dash in connection with other punctuation marks except a period; exceptions allow retention of a comma before the first dash when the parenthetical would otherwise require a comma, and retain interrogation or exclamation within the dashes when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect: 'Dear Sir: — I have...' Preferred: 'Dear Sir: I have...' But: commas may be retained before a first dash if the parenthetical omission would require a comma. Examples: Darwin, the promulgator of the theory, — though...; Senator Blank — shall we call him statesman or politician? — introduced the bill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses for enumerations and notation (176)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place figures or letters used to mark divisions in enumerations in parentheses run into the text. If paragraphed, use single parenthesis with lower-case italic letters and a period with figures and capital letters; follow a recommended scheme for syllabi indentation (A, I, 1, a), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The reasons for his resignation were three: (i) advanced age, (2) failing health, (3) a desire to travel.' and a full indention scheme is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit parentheses for parenthetical clauses (177)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid parentheses for parenthetical clauses unless confusion would arise from less distinctive marks or the clause is wholly irrelevant to the main argument; prefer dashes for relevant or integrated interpolations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use dashes for integrated parentheticals and parentheses for truly subordinate or editorial asides: 'He meant — I take this to be the (somewhat obscure) sense of his speech — that...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Brackets: uses and functions (178)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use brackets to enclose an explanation/note, indicate an interpolation in a quotation, rectify mistakes, supply omissions, or for parentheses within parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: editorial insertions [— Editor.], clarifications within quotes "These [the free-silver Democrats] asserted...", rectifications "the Italian [Englishman] Dante Gabriel Rossetti...", supplying omitted series details in bibliographic references, and nested parentheses in citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting continuation notices in brackets (179)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'To be continued' or 'Continued from...' at the end or beginning of articles/chapters should be placed between brackets, centered, italicized, and set in reduced type according to reduction rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: [Continued from p. 120], [To be concluded] (set in italics and reduced size).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses to indicate omission and lacunae (180)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ellipses to indicate omission from a quotation (words not essential to the conveyed idea), illegible words, mutilations, or other lacunae. Use four periods (separated by spaces/en quads) for ellipsis that include sentence boundaries; for whole-paragraph or line omissions insert a full line of periods separated by em- or 2-em quads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the preceding line ends in a point, do not include it in the four periods. In very narrow measures exceptions apply. In French, three periods only. Examples illustrate punctuation and spacing; in poetry insert line(s) of periods sized to line length and not extending beyond the longest type-line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis as part of citation: enclosed in quotation marks (181)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis used in a quotation should be treated as part of the citation and therefore enclosed within the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When omitting from a quotation include the ellipsis inside the quotation marks as part of the quoted material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen: general placement and tendency (182)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is used at line terminations when a syllable continues on the next line and between many compounds; modern tendency favors solid (closed) compounds rather than hyphenation, but many compounds remain better hyphenated. Apply judgment; rules provided cover common cases but are not absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of closed compounds: schoolroom, workshop, headquarters. Note: rules are guidelines; exercise judgment when applying them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compound adjectives before a noun (183)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate two or more words combined into a single adjective when placed before a noun or when the noun is understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: so-called Croesus, well-known author, first-class investment, better-trained teachers, high-school course, half-dead horse, English-speaking peoples, nineteenth-century progress, four-year-old boy, house-to-house canvass. Exceptions: New Testament times, Old English spelling, an a priori argument. If a component contains more than one word, use an en dash (New York–Chicago freight traffic). Do not hyphenate when the first component is an adverb ending in -ly or when following the noun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate noun compounds formed by two nouns in objective relation (184)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, hyphenate nouns formed by two nouns where one component is derived from a transitive verb (objective relation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mind-reader, story-teller, fool-killer, office-holder, well-wisher, property-owner; hero-worship, child-study, wood-turning. Exceptions include common brief compounds: lawgiver, taxpayer, proofreader, bookkeeper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate certain present-participle compounds (185)
rubrics_metrics.description: A present participle united with a noun to form a new noun, or with a preposition used absolutely to form a noun, may take a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: boarding-house, dining-hall, sleeping-room, dwelling-place, printing-office, walking-stick, starting-point, stepping-stone, stumbling-block.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds with book/house/mill/room/shop/work: hyphenation by syllable count (186)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds with 'book', 'house', 'mill', 'room', 'shop', 'work' are printed as one word when the prefixed noun has one syllable, hyphenated when it has two, and printed as two words when it has three or more (with some exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: handbook, schoolbook, notebook; pocket-book, story-book; boathouse, clubhouse, schoolhouse; engine-house, power-house; commill, handmill, sawmill; water-mill, paper-mill; bedroom, classroom, schoolroom; exceptions for appearance's sake: source-book, wheat-mill, school work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate occupational compounds and adjectival compounds before proper nouns (187)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'maker', 'dealer', etc., and nouns combined in an adjectival sense before a proper noun are ordinarily hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: harness-maker, book-dealer, job-printer; a soldier-statesman, the poet-artist Rossetti. Short everyday exceptions: bookmaker, dressmaker, shopgirl.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation rules for specific prefixes and particles (199-207, 209-213)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for prefixes, particles, negatives, and combining forms: 'half-', 'semi-', 'demi-', 'bi-' etc., use of hyphen with 'self-', 'fold', 'like', 'vice-', 'ex-', 'elect', negative particles, 'non-', 'quasi-', 'over/under' and Latin/Greek prepositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: 'half-', 'quarter-' require hyphen (half-truth); 'semi-','demi-' usually no hyphen unless followed by i, w, y or in unusual formations; 'self-' forms are hyphenated (self-evident); 'non-' ordinarily calls for hyphen except common words (nonessential); 'quasi-' requires hyphen; 'over'/'under' prefixes generally without hyphen except unusual cases; Latin/Greek prepositions usually omit hyphen except where combining with same terminal letter or to avoid diphthongs; 'co-','pre-','re-' take hyphen when followed by same vowel or by w or y (co-operation, re-enter), but usually omitted otherwise (coeducation). Note many exceptions for proper names and meaning distinctions (pre-Raphaelite, re-cover vs recover).

rubrics_metrics.name: List of commonly hyphenated everyday words (214)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a list of everyday words that should be hyphenated and that do not fall under earlier classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: after-years, anti-trust, bas-relief, birth-rate, blood-feud, coat-of-arms, cross-examine, death-rate, first-fruits, folk-song, good-will, page-proof, guinea-pig, horse-power, ice-cream, loan-word, son-in-law, subject-matter, title-page, wave-length, well-being, will-power, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary word divisions at line breaks (215)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid unnecessary divisions of words; wherever consistent with good spacing, carry the whole word over to the next line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer not to hyphenate if acceptable spacing can be maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on dividing very short syllables and words (216)
rubrics_metrics.description: In wide measures (20 ems or more), avoid dividing on a syllable of two letters; never carry over a syllable of two letters. Words of four letters should never be divided; five- or six-letter words rarely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: avoid dividing short words like ow/ly; maintain good spacing but avoid two-letter syllable splits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid consecutive lines ending in hyphens and bad breakline placement (217)
rubrics_metrics.description: Never allow more than two consecutive lines to terminate with a hyphen if avoidable; avoid a divided word at the next-to-last or last line of a paragraph and avoid division at the bottom of a recto page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The breakline (last line) in measures of 15 ems and up should contain at least four letters; manage layout to avoid unsightly division positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide proper nouns or separate initials (218-219)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide proper nouns (especially personal names) unless absolutely necessary, and do not separate initials or combinations like a.d., P.M., etc., across lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry the full name or initials together on one line where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep divisional marks with their following matter (220)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid separation of a divisional mark (e.g., (a) or (i)) from the section it precedes; do not allow such marks to fall at the end of a line but carry them over with the associated matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure enumerative markers stay attached to following text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide words according to American pronunciation, not derivation (221)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide words according to pronunciation (American system) rather than derivation (English system), while compatible with pronunciation and good spacing prefer division on etymological lines for compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred American divisions: democ-racy (not demo-cracy); knowl-edge (not know-ledge). For compounds prefer dis-pleasure rather than displeas-ure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division when consonants meet between vowels (222)
rubrics_metrics.description: When two consonants meet between vowels and the syllable ends on one consonant, division may be made between the consonants, with pronunciation determining the split.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: advan-tage, exces-sive, finan-cier, foun-da-tion, impor-tant, moun-tain, profes-sor, struc-ture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid terminating a line in soft c, g, or j (223)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid ending a line with a soft c, g, or j; if unavoidable, choose preferred splits rather than leaving awkward fragments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred divisions: pro-cess (not proc-ess), ne-cessary (not nec-essary), spacing (not spac-ing) — with the rule that present participle -ing should be carried over.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide on a vowel when practicable; exceptions for -able/-ible (224)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where practicable divide on a vowel; if a vowel alone forms a syllable in the middle of a word, run it into the first line. Exceptions: words in -able and -ible should carry the vowel into the next line (read-able, convert-ible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred: sepa-rate (not sep-arate); particu-lar (not partic-ular).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid additional hyphens in hyphenated nouns/adjectives (225)
rubrics_metrics.description: In hyphenated nouns and adjectives, avoid creating extra hyphens by dividing again across the hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: object-lesson, not object-les-son; fellow-being, not fel-low-being; poverty-stricken, not pover-ty-stricken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat diphthongs as one letter for division (226)
rubrics_metrics.description: A coalition of two vowel sounds (a diphthong) should be treated as one letter and not be split across lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not divide peo-ple, Cae-sar, bu-ilding; avoid splits that separate diphthongs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division for derivatives from words ending in -t (227)
rubrics_metrics.description: For derivatives from words ending in t, carry the t into the next line with the suffix if the accent shifts; if the derivative retains the parent's accent, leave the t in the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: objec-tive (from ob'ject), defect-ive (from defect'); but respec-tively, distinc-tive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural -s adding syllable doesn't justify division (228)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a plural s that creates a new syllable does not justify dividing the word differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not split words like hor-ses or circumstan-ces across the plural in awkward ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide adjectives ending in -ical on the 'i' (229)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives in -ical should be divided on the i (physi-cal), not phys-ical or physic-al.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure correct morphemic break for -ical adjectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide the word 'nothing' (230)
rubrics_metrics.description: Never divide the word 'nothing'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not hyphenate or split 'nothing' across lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language division rules summarized (231 introduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Condensed rules for dividing words in common foreign languages are provided and intended to cover ordinary contingencies encountered in proofreading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See the language-specific entries that follow for French, German, Italian, Spanish, Greek, and Latin rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: French division rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on vowels as far as possible, avoiding consonantal syllable endings; carry certain consonant pairs (where second is l or r) into the following syllable; count vowels for syllables (mute e exceptions); i,y,o,u before vowels often act as consonants and then do not form a syllable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in-di-vi-si-bi-li-te, a-che-ter; tableau (not tab-leau); two-consonant patterns: ta-bleau, e-cri-vain; e-taient, joue-rai; bien, yeux, fouet-ter illustrates vowel/consonant behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: German division rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on vowels as far as possible; when several consonants stand between vowels, usually carry only the last consonant over; do not separate certain clusters (sz, ch, sch, ph, st, th), with some exceptions; 'ck' when divided separates as k-k; in foreign words combinations of certain consonants with l or r are carried over; compound words separated first into their elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Fi-la-bri-k (illustrated), Rit-ter, klir-ren; Bu-sze, Be-cher, Haus-chen exceptions; Deckel — Dek-kel for ck; compounds like Fiirsten-schlosz apply component separation first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italian division rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on vowels as far as possible; do not separate s before consonant, r after consonant, or clusters ch, gh, gli, gn, qu, sc, cl, fl, gl, pi; i=y and u=w go with following vowel; certain vowel combinations are not separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ta-vo-li-no, nar-ra-re; ca-sti-ghi, mi-glio-re; miei, tuoi for vowel combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish division rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel as far as possible; treat certain consonant clusters as simple consonants following the vowel rule; ensure liquids (l and r) when preceded by another consonant are not separated from that consonant except in compounds; s is always disjoined from a following consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ca-ra-co-les, re-ba-no; mu-cha-cho, ba-ta-lla; ha-blar, po-dria, ce-le-bra-cion; cuer-da, chas-co, pron-to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek division rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Place single consonants and consonant combinations that can begin a word at the beginning of the following syllable; other consonant combinations are divided; compound words are divided into original parts first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative Greek transliteration examples indicate syllable breaks and treatment of consonant clusters and compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin division rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A Latin word has as many syllables as vowels or diphthongs; when a single consonant occurs between vowels, divide before the consonant; when two or more consonants occur, divide before the last consonant except for mute+liquid combinations and qu/gu; compound words first separated into elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cae-sar, me-ri-di-es; om-nis, scrip-tus (but pa-tris, e-quus); ad-est, ab-rum-po.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference index markers and superior figures in text (232)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use superior figures for reference indexes in text as a rule; use asterisks, daggers, etc., only in special cases (e.g., tables or algebraic matter). Index figures should be placed after punctuation without space, except in German where inside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When figures are not used, sequence of symbols: * (asterisk), † (dagger), ‡ (double dagger), § (section mark), || (parallels), ¶ (paragraph mark). Examples show placement of index markers relative to punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ihid., loc. cit., op. cit. for repeated references (233)
rubrics_metrics.description: When references to the same work follow each other closely and uninterruptedly, use 'Ibid.' instead of repeating the title; Ibid. replaces as much of the previous reference as is repeated. Avoid using Ibid. for the first footnote on a verso page; instead repeat the short title or use loc. cit. or op. cit. as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use Ibid. for repeated successive references; for verso-first footnote prefer repeating title or using loc. cit. (whole citation) or op. cit. (work only).

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes to tables and use of symbols (234)
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes to tables should be in 6-pt and placed at the foot of the table (not page); for reference indexes in tables use asterisks/daggers rather than superior figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always place table footnotes at foot of table; use typographic symbols in tables to avoid confusion from figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitting author's name in footnote when present in text (235)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author's name is given in the text in connection with a reference or quotation, do not repeat it in the footnote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shows how a footnote may simply contain the bibliographic details without repeating a name already present in the running text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of index figures relative to quotations (236)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferably place the index (footnote) figure in the text at the end of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example demonstrates placing the footnote marker after punctuation at the end of a quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations in references and numeral/punctuation conventions (237)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily omit 'Vol.', 'chap.', and 'p.' in references to particular passages; use Roman numerals for Volume/Book/Part/Division (capitals), lower-case roman for chapters and introductory matter, and Arabic numerals for numbers and text pages. Use 'Vol.' or 'p.' only when confusion might arise. Classical references use no comma between author's name and title and use periods in place of commas for divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Miller, French Rev. (2d ed.; London: Abrahams, 1888), II, Part IV, iii. Use conventions appropriate for classical vs modern references; where a page reference stands alone, use 'p.' or 'pp.'
